papers.title: Untitled
papers.abstract: Tick-borne pathogens are emerging across Southeast Asia, but their diversity and ecological drivers in Malaysia remain poorly understood. We screened 539 ixodid ticks collected from natural forests, marginal habitats, and oil palm plantations in Peninsular Malaysia for Rickettsia spp., Borrelia spp., and Orientia tsutsugamushi using PCR and phylogenetic analyses. Overall, 10.61% (7/66) of tick pools tested positive for bacterial pathogens. Rickettsia was detected in 4.55% (3/66) of pools from Dermacentor auratus and Amblyomma cordiferum, whereas Borrelia was detected in 6.06% (4/66) of pools from A. cordiferum, Haemaphysalis hystricis, and Ixodes granulatus. Orientia tsutsugamushi was not detected. Phylogenetic analyses placed the detected Rickettsia within ancestral and spotted fever groups and the detected Borrelia within Lyme disease and relapsing fever clades. Positive detections suggested habitat-specific patterns, with Borrelia identified only in forest-derived tick pools, Rickettsia detected in both forest and marginal habitats, and none of the targeted pathogens detected in plantation-derived pools. This study provides comparative molecular evidence of zoonotic tick-borne bacteria across contrasting landscapes in Peninsular Malaysia, establishing a baseline for future surveillance and underscoring the need to investigate how land-use change may influence pathogen transmission at the human-wildlife interface.

papers.title: Untitled
papers.abstract: A number of health care providers recommend the antibiotics rifampin, trimethoprim, and/or dapsone for treatment of Lyme disease. In opposition, previous studies found that Lyme disease-causing Borrelia are innately resistant to those antibiotics at concentrations that would be lethal to other bacterial species. To resolve those contradictions, multiple genospecies and strains of Lyme disease-causing spirochetes were assessed for their ability to grow and replicate in the presence of these drugs. For each antibiotic, the minimum concentrations necessary to prevent growth of Borrelia burgdorferi sensu stricto type strain B31 exceeded 300 µg/mL. All of the tested genospecies of Lyme disease, Borrelia, grew and replicated in the presence of 100 µg/mL or more of antibiotic. In contrast, prior studies determined that maximum serum concentrations of these antibiotics in humans and laboratory animals are less than 15 µg/mL. The current study's results indicate that rifampin, trimethoprim, and dapsone are unlikely to have any positive effect in clearing Lyme disease-causing Borrelia infections. There are conflicting reports on the efficacy of using the antibiotics rifampin, trimethoprim, or dapsone against the Lyme disease spirochete, Borrelia burgdorferi (sensu lato). The present studies found that the concentration of antibiotic necessary to prevent borrelial growth and replication, alone or in combination, exceeded 200 µg/mL for all tested strains of B. burgdorferi sensu lato. In contrast, previous studies of humans and mice found that clinically relevant dosages of these antibiotics yielded maximum serum concentrations of 15 µg/mL or less. All together, these data indicate that these pharmaceuticals are not likely to be effective in curing B. burgdorferi (sl) infections.

papers.title: Untitled
papers.abstract: Lyme disease is a tick-borne disease primarily caused by the bacterium Borrelia burgdorferi (Bb). Following a tick bite, Bb is injected into the dermis and colonizes the local tissue, where it can spread to distant organs through the vascular system. Although dissemination is a crucial factor in disease progression, our understanding of the mechanisms and factors that affect Bb dissemination through circulation is incomplete. To assess the role of wall shear stress (WSS) on Bb adhesion and extravasation, we perfused a 3D tissue-engineered microvessel with fluorescently labeled Bb at different wall shear stresses. The rate of Bb adhesion and extravasation from the microvessel was strongly dependent on WSS. Bb adhered to the endothelium in an elongated morphology and occasionally exhibited "flipping" events with one end of the Bb anchored and the other end detaching and reattaching downstream. Finally, circulating Bb did not induce endothelial activation following 6 h of perfusion, although increased microvessel permeability at low WSS was correlated with increased Bb adhesion events. Our results provide a new approach to investigating Bb dissemination and offers new insights into the mechanisms of Bb extravasation.IMPORTANCEFollowing a tick bite, Borrelia burgdorferi (Bb), the causative agent for Lyme disease, can disseminate to distant organs through the vascular system. Here, we utilize a 3D tissue-engineered microvessel model to gain insight into how wall shear stress (WSS) impacts Bb extravasation and Bb migration behavior across endothelial cells. During perfusion, Bb transiently adhered to the endothelium prior to detaching or extravasating into the surrounding extracellular matrix. The number of adhesion events was strongly dependent on WSS, and extravasation events were only observed at the lowest WSS. Adherent Bb were usually elongated and aligned in the direction of flow, and did not exhibit the helical morphology associated with migration under static conditions or in the extracellular matrix. Adherent Bb exhibited "flipping" events in which the back (upstream) end of the Bb detached and subsequently reattached downstream, becoming the front end while the other end remained anchored to the endothelium.

papers.title: Iron sourcing strategies and adaptive protein responses to iron deprivation in the intraerythrocytic parasite Babesia divergens.
papers.abstract: Iron is indispensable for the survival and pathogenicity of Babesia parasites, yet the mechanisms underlying its acquisition remain largely unresolved. In contrast to other apicomplexan parasites, tick-borne Babesia species rapidly lose the parasitophorous vacuole following erythrocyte invasion and do not form hemozoin, suggesting the evolution of distinct strategies for iron metabolism. Here, we demonstrate that Babesia divergens utilizes a sequential, multi-route iron acquisition system to meet its metabolic demands within host erythrocytes. Kinetic uptake analyses reveal a pronounced preference for ferrous iron (Fe2+), which is imported through an active, energy-dependent process supported by extracellular ferric reductase activity that converts host-derived ferric iron (Fe3+) into a bioavailable form prior to uptake. Using immunogold transmission electron microscopy, we provide evidence for the active internalization of host transferrin and show that parasite proliferation is dose-dependently inhibited by apo-transferrin, establishing iron as a limiting factor for parasite growth. Quantitative proteomic profiling revealed a limited, stage-specific response to deferoxamine-induced iron deprivation. Three proteins showed statistically significant changes in abundance in free merozoites: the conserved multipass membrane protein Bdiv_019230 increased, whereas the hypothetical protein Bdiv_002300 and the putative serine hydroxymethyltransferase Bdiv_027330 decreased. No proteins reached the statistical significance threshold in intraerythrocytic parasites. These results identify a small set of statistically supported candidates for investigating the response of extracellular B. divergens merozoites to iron-restricted conditions.

papers.title: Untitled
papers.abstract: Following a tick bite, Borrelia burgdorferi spirochetes replicate in human skin and disseminate through tissues, including subcutaneous adipose tissue. Adipose is a complex organ containing both immune and non-immune cells that play a significant role in the immune response, yet little is known about adipose-specific immune signaling after B. burgdorferi infection. We investigated the landscape of immune signaling within adipose tissue-resident cells during B. burgdorferi infection in human tissue (skin and adipose tissue) ex vivo. Single-cell sequencing pathway analysis revealed upregulation of inflammatory pathways in skin, yet overall downregulation of immune pathways in adipose tissue cells during B. burgdorferi infection. Adipose-resident myeloid cells and adipose stem/progenitor cells (ASPCs) displayed an inflammatory profile characterized by the increased expression of IL-1β, TNF, and NFKB1. CellChat, a cellular communication comparative analysis, showed increased cell-to-cell communication across adipose-resident cell populations. ASPCs demonstrated the strongest outgoing signals, positioning them as key hubs of intercellular communication in adipose tissue. Interestingly, we observed adipose-specific downregulation of serum amyloid A (SAA), an inflammatory serum marker known to have antimicrobial properties and typically elevated in Lyme disease patients during acute infection. Therefore, we further evaluated the interaction between SAA and B. burgdorferi. Here, we show that human recombinant SAA protein directly binds B. burgdorferi spirochetes, reduces spirochete viability in a dose-dependent manner in vitro, and enhances phagocytosis. Taken together, these findings show that adipose tissue is a site of active immune signaling in the setting of infection and identify SAA as a host defense factor against B. burgdorferi.IMPORTANCEBorrelia burgdorferi is the bacterium that is transmitted by ticks and causes Lyme disease. These bacteria replicate in the skin to cause the localized skin rash erythema migrans, then disseminate to cause symptoms in other organs, including the joints and heart. Adipose tissue, or fat, is adjacent to skin, joints, and heart-all target organs of infection. In this study, we set out to understand how adipose tissue/fat plays a role in Lyme disease. We discovered that B. burgdorferi infection leads to an immune response in adipose tissue cells with specific downregulation of a gene called serum amyloid A (SAA). Our work shows that B. burgdorferi bacteria bind serum amyloid A (SAA), leading to decreased viability in vitro and enhanced uptake of B. burgdorferi by white blood cells. These findings highlight the dynamic role our fat can play during B. burgdorferi infection and can lead to the identification of new treatments for Lyme disease.

papers.title: Detection of vector-borne organisms in domestic cats in the United States and Canada (2019 - 2025) with analysis of Hepatozoon variants.
papers.abstract: Published large-scale vector-borne organism (VBO) PCR prevalence studies in domestic cats are limited. The prevalence of VBOs in feline blood samples submitted for PCR testing by a veterinary diagnostic laboratory between January 2, 2019, and December 23, 2025 (n = 7581) was determined. Feline blood samples were tested for Anaplasma, Apicomplexa, Babesia, Bartonella, Cytauxzoon, Ehrlichia, hemotropic Mycoplasma, and Rickettsia. VBOs were detected in 1373/7581 (18.1%) blood samples, with Mycoplasma haemominutum (8.87%) and Bartonella henselae (5.99%) being the most prevalent. Hepatozoon spp. were identified in 40 (0.58%) cats, prompting further genetic and epidemiologic characterization. Sequence analysis of a 182-bp fragment of the Hepatozoon 18S rRNA gene from 40 PCR-positive cats identified seven haplotypes with the highest sequence similarities to Hepatozoon silvestris, Hepatozoon felis, and bobcat-associated Hepatozoon spp. Phylogenetic analysis resolved the variants into major groups clustering with H. silvestris, H. felis, and nondomestic felid-associated Hepatozoon spp. Most Hepatozoon-positive cats originated from the Northeast and Mid-Atlantic regions of the United States (34/40; 85.0%), of which seven infections (7/40; 17.5%) involved cats undergoing blood donor screening. Overall, PCR testing confirmed infection with a VBO in approximately one in five cats tested in the U.S and Canada. Hepatozoon infections were more common than previously recognized, underscoring the value of Hepatozoon-specific PCR in feline VBO diagnostic testing.

papers.title: Babesia blood donor screening: A tool for safety and surveillance.
papers.abstract: Babesia is a transfusion-transmissible, tick-borne parasite endemic in the northeastern and upper midwestern US. Since 2020, nucleic acid test screening of blood donations has been implemented in endemic areas to reduce transfusion-transmitted babesiosis. American Red Cross blood donations collected between May 2020 and April 2026 in 13 endemic states and Washington, DC, were screened using the FDA-licensed Procleix Babesia transcription-mediated amplification assay. Reactive donations were analyzed by season, geography, donor characteristics, and state-level reactivity rates. Incidence estimates were evaluated using rolling 2-year periods. About 10 million donations were screened, of which 2505 were Babesia-reactive. Overall donor reactivity increased significantly from 0.02% during 2020-2021 to 0.03% during 2021-2026 (p < .001). Significant increases were observed in Maine, New York, and Pennsylvania, and no state demonstrated a significant decline. Donation reactivity exhibited a consistent seasonal pattern, while geographic analyses showed expansion of donor reactivity across the northeastern US, particularly along the eastern seaboard. Incidence increased from 63.2 to 71.0 per 100,000 person-years across the study period, with sustained increases in several states. Among 1638 reinstated donors, 59% returned to donate and 2% tested reactive again, suggesting persistent infection or reinfection. Six years of routine Babesia screening have effectively protected the blood supply while providing valuable surveillance for asymptomatic infection. Rising donor reactivity, expanding geographic distribution, and evidence of persistent or recurrent infection indicate an increasing risk of babesiosis in the United States and support continued screening and surveillance.

papers.title: Pediatric Musculoskeletal Infections: Who Needs a Tap or MRI? From Kocher to PEMCRC.
papers.abstract: Bacterial musculoskeletal infections (MSKIs), including septic arthritis, osteomyelitis, and pyomyositis, are challenging diagnoses to make in pediatric emergency medicine because their presentation frequently overlaps with more common conditions, including transient synovitis, Lyme arthritis, reactive arthritis, and other inflammatory arthritides. While delayed diagnosis may result in significant morbidity, over-testing may expose children to invasive procedures, advanced imaging, sedation, hospitalization, and unnecessary antimicrobial therapy. Pediatric emergency clinicians must therefore balance the competing risks of missed infection and excessive diagnostic evaluation and treatment. Numerous tools exist to aid clinicians, including blood biomarkers-white blood cell (WBC) count, absolute neutrophil count (ANC), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), C-reactive protein (CRP), and procalcitonin (PCT). However, blood biomarkers have limited diagnostic accuracy when used in isolation. To address this limitation, clinical prediction tools that combine laboratory values with clinical features to stratify risk have been developed. In this review, we summarize the data for clinically available biomarkers and clinical prediction tools for the evaluation of pediatric bacterial MSKIs and discuss their practical application, limitations, and integration into clinical decision-making in the emergency department (ED). Ultimately, we provide a framework to help pediatric emergency clinicians identify children who require advanced testing and interventions while avoiding unnecessary evaluation and treatment in low-risk patients.

papers.title: Persistent Borrelia burgdorferi Peptidoglycan in Postinfectious Lyme Arthritis: Innate Immune Sensing and Translational Implications.
papers.abstract: Lyme arthritis (LA) is the late articular manifestation of Borrelia burgdorferi infection. It is ordinarily treated successfully with appropriate antibiotic therapy. In a subset of patients, however, synovitis persists for months to years after treatment, despite presumed eradication of the spirochete. This state is termed postinfectious, or antibiotic-refractory, LA, and its cellular and molecular basis remains incompletely defined. It is distinct from post-treatment Lyme disease syndrome (PTLDS), which is defined by persistent subjective symptoms without objective joint inflammation. Attention has increasingly turned to the non-canonical peptidoglycan (PG) of B. burgdorferi. Three questions are central: what becomes of this material during bacterial growth, whether it persists within the joint after antimicrobial treatment, and whether it can engage innate immune sensing pathways such as NOD2. Whether such sensing occurs in the human joint has yet to be established. This narrative review synthesizes the available human, murine, and in vitro mechanistic evidence on four topics: B. burgdorferi PG biology, PG processing in both the bacterium and the host, the innate mechanisms of PG recognition, and the intersection of these pathways with adaptive autoimmune mechanisms in postinfectious LA. Throughout, findings established in patients are distinguished from inferences drawn from murine models and from hypotheses that remain unsupported by patient-level data. Human evidence is limited to detection of PG in synovial fluid from closely related research groups and is not independently replicated, together with genetic, immunologic, and tissue studies that do not themselves address PG. Findings such as PG tropism for the liver and NOD2 sensing derive from murine and in vitro systems. No study has shown that persistent PG or NOD2 signaling causes human postinfectious synovitis. The authors then consider the translational implications for diagnostic, prognostic, and anti-inflammatory or PG-directed strategies as hypotheses.

papers.title: One Health approach to Babesia and Bartonella species: occupational zoonotic infections in veterinary workers and their families.
papers.abstract: This study investigated the presence of Babesia, Bartonella, and Borrelia spp infection in an extended veterinary family. Between May 2023 and August 2025, 8 individuals enrolled in an Institutional Review Board-approved observational study. Serological evidence of Bartonella spp exposure and molecular evidence of Babesia, Bartonella, and Borrelia spp infection were assessed. Among other symptoms, at least half of the study participants reported chronic fatigue, headaches, anxiety, depression, and difficulty remembering. On the basis of PCR amplification and DNA sequencing, infection with Babesia odocoilei, Babesia divergens-like MO-1, Babesia gibsoni, or Babesia microti was confirmed in 4 individuals. Three other individuals were PCR positive for Piroplasmida/Apicomplexa DNA. Four individuals were seroreactive to 1 or more Bartonella spp and 6 individuals were Bartonella PCR positive in blood, serum, or enrichment blood cultures. Six individuals had at least 1 Borrelia partition detected by digital PCR; however, efforts in our laboratory to confirm Borrelia digital PCR positivity by DNA sequencing were not successful. Similar to this extended veterinary family, previous studies have documented that veterinarians and veterinary workers may be occupationally at risk for exposure to Bartonella spp. On the basis of the results of this study, veterinary workers may also be at risk for infection with Babesia spp and potentially other Piroplasmida/Apicomplexa organisms. The potential that chronic intravascular or endotheliotropic infections with vector-borne pathogens contributes to multisystem illnesses in veterinary workers deserves future research considerations, which, on a clinical, epidemiological, and microbiological basis, will require sequential lifetime studies.

papers.title: Bacterial diversity associated with Streblidae flies parasitizing cave-dwelling bats from northeastern Brazil.
papers.abstract: Bats (Chiroptera) are highly diverse mammals that play key ecological roles and harbor a wide range of microorganisms, yet the microbiome of their ectoparasitic flies remains poorly understood. This study characterized and compared the bacterial microbiomes associated with two bat-ectoparasite systems, Pteronotus gymnonotus-Trichobius johnsonae and Desmodus rotundus-Trichobius parasiticus, from cave-dwelling bat populations in northeastern Brazil using 16S rRNA gene sequencing. Sixty-eight bat fly samples were successfully sequenced, and 67 were retained for downstream ecological analyses after quality filtering. Bacterial communities were dominated by members of the classes Gammaproteobacteria and Alphaproteobacteria, with Arsenophonus, Bartonella, and unresolved endosymbiont-associated taxa among the most abundant bacterial groups. Alpha-diversity patterns varied according to the metric considered: observed ASV richness was influenced by bat fly species, sex, and their interaction, Shannon diversity differed according to streblid fly species and sex, and Faith's phylogenetic diversity differed between bat fly sexes. Notably, male T. johnsonae exhibited greater observed ASV richness than females, whereas no significant sex difference was detected in T. parasiticus. Beta-diversity analyses consistently revealed differences in bacterial community composition between the two bat-ectoparasite systems, while the influence of sex was system-dependent, with significant differentiation between T. johnsonae males and females but not between sexes of T. parasiticus in phylogenetically informed analyses. Differential abundance analysis further identified Romboutsia, Bartonella, Bacteroides, and an unclassified Pseudomonadota genus as discriminatory taxa among groups. Overall, these findings reveal distinct bacterial diversity and composition patterns between the two bat-ectoparasite systems and indicate that sex-associated microbiome variation is not uniform across bat fly species.
papers.journal: Comparative immunology, microbiology and infectious diseases

papers.title: Diversity and distribution of Bartonella spp. in domestic animals, wildlife, and ectoparasites in Brazil: a comprehensive review.
papers.abstract: Bartonella are intracellular Gram-negative blood-borne bacteria capable of infecting a wide range of hosts, primarily mammals and birds. They are responsible for emerging and re-emerging infectious diseases characterized by persistent intraerythrocytic bacteremia in mammals. Out of 49 species described, 13 presents zoonotic potential. This review aimed to update the current knowledge on the occurrence, distribution, and genetic diversity of Bartonella in domestic animals, wild mammals and birds, and ectoparasites in Brazil. A total of 72 scientific articles published between 2007 and 2026 were included. The available information indicates that the Southeastern and Central-Western regions of Brazil account for most reports of Bartonella in animals and ectoparasites, whereas the Northern and Northeastern regions remain comparatively understudied. Overall, studies investigating Bartonella in Brazil have become increasingly frequent and geographically widespread over the years. Although some investigations rely on single-gene analyses, most employ multi-locus sequence analysis and phylogenetic reconstruction, providing stronger evidence for species identification and diversity. In contrast, relatively few studies have incorporated whole-genome sequencing or comprehensive phenotypic and biochemical characterization through bacterial isolation and blood culture. Future research should prioritize advanced genomic approaches and bacterial isolation to improve our understanding of the diversity, evolution, and epidemiology of Bartonella circulating in Brazil.

papers.title: Molecular Screening of Arthropod-Borne Pathogens in Domestic Cats from Northeast of Mexico: First Report of Infection and Coinfection in the Country.
papers.abstract: Cat-associated pathogens transmitted by arthropods are of global public and veterinary health importance. Cats, as well as dogs, have historically coexisted with humans in rural and urban environments. However, studies on microorganisms associated with cats are much less extensive than those on dogs. Therefore, the present study aims to document natural infections of Anaplasma, Bartonella, Ehrlichia, and Rickettsia in cats (Felis catus) using PCR in northeastern Mexico. Blood samples were collected from cats with the support of the Canine and Feline Control Centers and veterinary clinics. Specific pathogens were amplified by PCR, and some positive samples were sequenced. A total of 250 cats were obtained from three municipalities in Nuevo Leon, Mexico. Specific PCR testing showed that 33.6% (84/250) cats tested positive for at least one of the pathogens. The overall natural pathogen infection rates were Ehrlichia with 20.8% (52/250), followed by Anaplasma with 8% (20/250), Bartonella with 3.2% (8/250), and Rickettsia with 1.6% (4/250). Phylogenetic analysis placed the Bartonella sequence within a well-supported B. quintana clade. The partial 16S rRNA sequence obtained from Ehrlichia was conservatively classified as Ehrlichia sp. closely related to E. chaffeensis. These findings document exposure or infection of cats with multiple arthropod-borne bacteria and support continued molecular surveillance using additional discriminatory loci.
papers.journal: Vector borne and zoonotic diseases (Larchmont, N.Y.)

papers.title: Circulating IP-10/CXCL10 Correlates With Parasitemia and Disease Severity in Patients With Babesiosis: A Pilot Study.
papers.abstract: Human babesiosis is an emerging tick-borne zoonosis that can cause serious complications, including death. Immune mechanisms that confer protection or promote disease severity in human babesiosis are poorly understood. We measured the cytokine and antibody profile in a cohort of hospitalized patients who had babesiosis. Cytokine levels were measured in plasma using the Bio-Plex Pro Human Cytokine 27-Plex Assay, and Babesia microti-specific total IgG and its 4 isotypes were measured using an immunofluorescence assay. Cytokine profile was analyzed in relation to immune status, peak parasitemia, lowest hemoglobin levels, and disease severity. There were enhanced levels of 8 cytokines (eotaxin, IL-6, IL-8, IL-10, IP-10/CXCL10, MCP-1, MIP-1α, and TNF-α) in the plasma of 16 patients with babesiosis as compared with 7 controls. A positive correlation was found between IP-10 levels and parasitemia (Spearman R = 0.52, P = .04). Patients with severe babesiosis had elevated levels of IP-10 and IL-5 as compared with the other 2 clinical categories (ie, moderate and moderately severe). Immunosuppression was associated with low levels of the VEGF and FGF basic angiogenic factors. There was also an inverse correlation between hemoglobin and IL-1β or IL-9 levels. Last, patients with babesiosis produced abundant levels of immunofluorescence assay total IgG and IgG1 and IgG3 but low levels of IgG2 and no IgG4. IP-10 and other cytokines that exhibited elevated levels should be further investigated as biomarkers of severe babesiosis.

papers.title: Phylogenetic Profiling and Molecular Detection of Babesia and Theileria spp. in Ticks Infesting Livestock Across Kashmir Valley, India.
papers.abstract: Ticks are major vectors of protozoan hemoparasites, particularly Babesia and Theileria, causing substantial morbidity and economic losses in livestock. Data on molecular prevalence and circulating species in the high-altitude Kashmir Valley are limited. This study investigated the prevalence, distribution, and phylogenetic relationships of piroplasm infections in ticks infesting domestic ruminants. A cross-sectional survey was conducted across eight districts of the Kashmir Valley. A total of 4,965 livestock animals were examined, of which 1,800 were found tick-infested, yielding an overall infestation rate of 36.27%. Collected ticks were morphologically identified and screened for Babesia and Theileria DNA using genus-specific 18 S rRNA PCR. Positive amplicons were sequenced and subjected to phylogenetic analysis. Of the 1,800 ticks examined, Haemaphysalis constituted 1,529 (84.0%), followed by Rhipicephalus 171 (9.5%) and Ornithodoros 100 (5.5%). Overall PCR positivity was 19/1,800 (1.06%) for Babesia spp. and 10/1,800 (0.56%) for Theileria spp. Babesia DNA was detected in ticks from cattle (3/720; 0.42%), sheep (14/720; 1.94%), and goats (2/360; 0.56%), whereas Theileria DNA was detected in ticks from cattle (5/720; 0.69%) and goats (5/360; 1.39%). Female ticks showed significantly higher Babesia positivity than males (13/648; 2.01% vs. 3/792; 0.38%; P = 0.004). Tick infestation peaked during summer months. Phylogenetic analysis showed that the Kashmir Babesia sequences clustered with B. bovis reference sequences, while the Theileria sequences clustered with T. cf. luwenshuni-related sequences. This molecular and phylogenetic study provides evidence of B. bovis and T. luwenshuni-like sequences in ticks collected from livestock in the Kashmir Valley. Haemaphysalis was the predominant tick genus associated with the detected piroplasmid infections. Although overall PCR positivity was low, the findings provide baseline data for piroplasm surveillance and support further characterization using higher-resolution molecular markers.

papers.title: Ecological niche partitioning and urbanization-driven restructuring of flea-borne pathogen communities in stray carnivores of Peninsular Malaysia: discovery of uncharacterised Bartonella lineages.
papers.abstract: Flea-borne bacteria are emerging zoonotic pathogens of increasing public health importance, yet their ecological distribution, community structure, and genetic diversity across contrasting landscapes in Southeast Asia remain poorly understood. This study investigated flea infestation, flea-borne bacterial pathogens, and their ecological associations in stray cats and dogs across urban, peri-urban, and rural landscapes of Peninsular Malaysia. A total of 296 stray cats and dogs were examined for flea infestation, and all recovered fleas (n = 636) were identified morphologically and screened individually for Bartonella spp., Rickettsia spp., and Orientia tsutsugamushi using polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assays followed by Sanger sequencing and phylogenetic analysis. Risk factors associated with flea infestation, Bartonella spp. and Rickettsia spp. occurrence were evaluated using generalized linear models (GLMs), generalized linear mixed-effects models (GLMMs), and Firth's penalized logistic regression, respectively. Pathogen community structure was assessed using alpha diversity indices, non-metric multidimensional scaling (NMDS), permutational multivariate analysis of variance (PERMANOVA), and tripartite ecological network analysis. Overall flea infestation prevalence was 32.09% (95/296), with infestation significantly higher in cats (39.44%) than dogs (13.25%) (χ2 = 10.672, df = 1, p = 0.001). All 636 fleas exhibited complete host-associated segregation, with Ctenocephalides felis (n = 485) occurring exclusively on cats and C. orientis (n = 151) exclusively on dogs. Flea-borne pathogens were detected in 71.86% (457/636) of fleas, comprising Bartonella henselae, B. clarridgeiae, B. koehlerae, several uncharacterized Bartonella lineages, Rickettsia felis, and R. asembonensis. Urban landscapes were associated with significantly higher Bartonella prevalence in C. felis (70.05%), whereas C. orientis was overwhelmingly dominated by R. asembonensis (94.04%). Ecological analyses demonstrated significant landscape-associated variation in pathogen community composition among C. felis populations but not C. orientis. Phylogenetic analysis identified a distinct, well-supported clade of previously uncharacterized Bartonella lineages (bootstrap = 100%). No O. tsutsugamushi was detected in any flea sample. Flea-borne pathogen communities in Peninsular Malaysia are structured by strong host-vector associations and ecological landscape, with peri-urban environments supporting greater pathogen diversity and urban landscapes demonstrated higher detection of Bartonella in C. felis. The discovery of previously uncharacterized Bartonella lineages expands the known diversity of flea-associated Bartonella in Malaysia and highlights the importance of integrating molecular epidemiology with community ecology to improve surveillance of emerging flea-borne zoonoses.

papers.title: Untitled
papers.abstract: The family Borreliaceae comprises the genera Cristispira and Borrelia, the latter including the subgenera Borrelia and Borreliella. Australia hosts a unique assemblage of wildlife and tick species that may support the circulation of indigenous Borrelia lineages. A narrative review of the available literature was conducted to summarize current knowledge of the taxonomy, diversity, ecology, tick associations, vertebrate hosts, and potential public health significance of Borreliaceae detected in Australia. The diversity of Australian Borrelia is currently represented by members of the relapsing fever (RF) and Echidna-Reptile (REP) groups. These include Borrelia queenslandica, Borrelia sp. HB, Candidatus Borrelia tachyglossi, Ca. B. undatumii, and Ca. B. rubricentralis, which have been detected in association with native wildlife and tick species. However, vector competence has not yet been demonstrated for most tick-associated Borrelia lineages identified in Australia. To date, no indigenous member of the Borrelia burgdorferi sensu lato complex has been convincingly detected in Australian ticks, wildlife, or humans. Nevertheless, persistent symptom complexes following tick exposure have been reported and are currently grouped under the umbrella term Debilitating Symptom Complexes Attributed to Ticks (DSCATT). Current evidence indicates that Australian Borreliaceae fauna is dominated by indigenous relapsing fever and reptile-associated lineages rather than Lyme borreliosis agents. Further genomic, ecological, reservoir-host, and vector-competence studies are needed to clarify their transmission cycles, evolutionary relationships, zoonotic potential, and their significance within a One Health framework.

papers.title: Untitled
papers.abstract: The tropical rat mite, Ornithonyssus bacoti (Hirst, 1913), is an obligate hematophagous gamasid mite of global veterinary, animal, and public health importance. While traditionally recognized as a cause of rodent mite dermatitis in humans, its potential involvement in zoonotic pathogen transmission requires rigorous critical evaluation. This paper provides a comprehensive review of research progress on O. bacoti, synthesizing evidence retrieved from major databases regarding its taxonomy, morphological diagnostics, life history, ecology, pathogen associations, genetic and physiological features, and integrated management. Morphologically, O. bacoti is distinguished from sibling species (O. sylviarum and O. bursa) by its long central dorsal setae, narrow tapering dorsal shield, and specific sternal plate setation. Under optimal laboratory conditions (28 °C, 75% relative humidity), its life cycle completes in 7-14 days, exhibiting arrhenotokous parthenogenesis. Epidemiologically, O. bacoti is a proven vector of Rickettsia akari (the causative agent of rickettsialpox) and serves as an intermediate host for the rodent filarial nematode Litomosoides sigmodontis. However, its role in transmitting Hantaviruses, Bartonella species, and other pathogens remains largely restricted to molecular detection or laboratory vector competence models, lacking definitive proof of natural transmission to humans. Furthermore, genomic insights remain preliminary, reliance on extrapolation from related poultry mites (Dermanyssus gallinae) must be carefully contextualized, and field resistance to pyrethroids warrants systematic monitoring. Effective mitigation requires a One Health strategy integrating host reduction, environmental sanitation, targeted acaricide use, and active vector surveillance.

papers.title: Vector-borne zoonotic bacteria in Tunisia: from fragmented data to an integrated One Health surveillance framework.
papers.abstract: Vector-borne and vector-associated bacterial zoonoses represent an important component of infectious disease epidemiology in Tunisia. This review synthesizes available evidence on major bacterial groups, including Rickettsia, Bartonella, Anaplasma, Ehrlichia, Borrelia, Coxiella burnetii, and other arthropod-associated bacteria, using a One Health framework integrating human, animal, vector, wildlife, and environmental compartments. The available evidence reveals heterogeneous levels of knowledge across bacterial taxa. Rickettsia represents the most established tick-associated zoonotic system, with Rickettsia conorii as the main confirmed human pathogen, while additional species have been detected mainly in arthropods or animal-associated settings. Bartonella has a significant clinical association with blood culture-negative endocarditis, whereas other bacterial groups show predominantly animal- or vector-associated evidence. Coxiella burnetii remains a major zoonotic concern linked to livestock, camels, reproductive materials, and environmental exposure. For Borrelia, Anaplasma, and Ehrlichia, substantial evidence of circulation exists in vectors and animals, but human clinical relevance remains incompletely characterized. Across bacterial groups, a recurrent limitation is the imbalance between molecular detection in vectors or animal hosts and confirmed evidence of transmission or human disease. Detection of bacterial DNA should therefore be interpreted cautiously and not considered equivalent to infection, reservoir competence, or vectorial transmission. Additional arthropod-associated bacteria identified through microbiome studies require further investigation to clarify their ecological significance. The Tunisian evidence base demonstrates active circulation of diverse vector-associated bacteria but remains fragmented across clinical, veterinary, entomological, and ecological domains. Strengthening integrated One Health surveillance through coordinated human diagnosis, animal sentinel systems, vector monitoring, environmental investigations, and advanced molecular approaches is essential to better assess zoonotic risks in Tunisia and the wider North African-Mediterranean region.

papers.title: Honey Bees as Bioindicators of Environmental PFASs Contamination and Potential Effects on Gut-Microbial Communities.
papers.abstract: Honey bees are valuable bioindicators of environmental contamination due to their wide foraging range and exposure to diverse biotic and abiotic stressors. This study evaluates the use of honey bees as bioindicators for detecting per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFASs) in areas with varying levels of exposure risk (high-, intermediate-, and low-), as well as their potential effects on gut-microbial communities. Analytical chemistry to detect PFASs and pesticide residues were combined with molecular and metagenomic analyses to identify common honey bee pathogens and characterize gut-microbial communities. Short-chain PFASs were predominated over long-chain compounds, particularly in high-risk areas, while pesticide residues occurred in only a few apiaries. Molecular analyses revealed several widespread pathogens, while metagenomics showed a stable gut microbiome mainly composed of the genera Lactobacillus, Bartonella, Bombilactobacillus, Snodgrassella, Gilliamella, Bifidobacterium, and Gluconacetobacter. However, microbial-community composition differed significantly between apiaries with high- versus low-risk PFAS exposure. These results support honey bees as effective bioindicators for environmental PFAS monitoring and suggest that PFAS exposure may be associated with alterations in their gut-microbial communities. Further research is needed to elucidate the impact of PFASs on honey bee toxicity, gut-microbiota composition, and overall health.

papers.title: Untitled
papers.abstract: Lyme neuroborreliosis (LNB), caused by Borrelia garinii, often leads to persistent neurological deficits, yet early diagnosis remains insensitive and the temporal metabolic changes in the infected brain are largely unexplored. In this study, a murine model of B. garinii infection was established using 80 female BALB/c mice, and brain tissues were collected at acute 7 (days post-infection, DPI), mid- (15 and 21 DPI), and chronic (30 DPI) stages for untargeted gas chromatography-time-of-flight mass spectrometry (GC-TOF-MS) metabolomics. Thirty-one differential metabolites were identified, with downregulated metabolites predominating acutely and upregulated metabolites prevailing chronically. Twelve common metabolites, including creatine, lysine, and galactose derivatives, were consistently altered. KEGG analysis revealed disrupted amino acid metabolism, particularly valine, leucine, and isoleucine biosynthesis (ko00290), arginine and proline metabolism (ko00330), and aminoacyl-tRNA biosynthesis (ko00970). ROC analysis identified five candidate biomarkers, hydroxylamine, 2,3-dihydroxypyridine, galactose 1, galactose 2, and monostearin, with high diagnostic accuracy. This study provides a comprehensive temporal metabolomic landscape of the brain during B. garinii infection, revealing time-dependent metabolic reprogramming with sustained disruptions in amino acid and energy metabolism, and offering candidate biomarkers for improved diagnosis of central nervous system involvement in Lyme disease.

papers.title: Retrospective Serological Survey of Equine Influenza Virus and Piroplasm Parasites in Free-Ranging Wild Equids from Kenya and Tanzania.
papers.abstract: Wild equids may act as reservoirs for infectious pathogens affecting domestic equine populations, yet data on exposure to equine infectious anemia virus (EIAV), equine influenza virus (EIV), and equine piroplasmosis agents in African wildlife remain scarce. Our objectives were to retrospectively determine serological evidence of exposure to EIAV, EIV, Theileria equi, and Babesia caballi among Grevy's zebras and rhinoceroses from Kenya and Tanzania. A total of 284 archived serum samples from 215 Grevy's zebras and 69 rhinoceroses were analyzed using commercial ELISAs. Positive EIAV screening tests were retested using a second confirmatory assay. No confirmed EIAV antibodies were detected in zebras or rhinoceroses. Antibodies against EIV were identified in 20/215 zebras (9.3%), all originating from Serengeti National Park. Theileria equi antibodies were detected in 194/206 zebras (94.2%), while Babesia caballi antibodies were detected in 8/206 zebras (3.9%). Rhinoceroses were negative for all pathogens tested. This study provides evidence of widespread exposure of Grevy's zebras to T. equi and limited exposure to EIV in East Africa while failing to identify serologic evidence of EIAV infection in zebras or rhinoceroses. These findings improve understanding of infectious disease ecology at the wildlife-livestock interface and support continued wildlife surveillance programs.

papers.title: A SAGA-like AP2-P-ARP1-GCN5 transcriptional complex targets pathogenesis-associated genes during the blood-stage development of Babesia gibsoni.
papers.abstract: Babesiosis is an increasingly recognized tick-borne zoonosis. The asexual blood stage of its causative agent, Babesia, drives pathological damages in the host and can cause severe or fatal human infections. Nevertheless, the transcriptional regulatory mechanisms that control this developmental stage remain poorly characterized. Here, we identified a novel ApiAP2 transcription factor (AP2-P; pathogenesis), which is essential in the blood-stage development of B. gibsoni. Nuclear import of AP2-P is inhibited by ivermectin, which is likely mediated via the IMPα/β pathway. Importantly, AP2-P forms a SAGA-like complex with the histone acetyltransferase GCN5 and a novel AP2-P related protein 1 (ARP1). Conditional knockdown of ARP1 or GCN5 results in reduced parasite growth rates accompanied by alterations in expression profiles and chromatin accessibility of pathogenesis-related genes. ChIP-seq data indicate that the complex associates with both euchromatic regions marked by H3K9ac and heterochromatic regions marked by H3K9me3, and it also targets many pathogenic genes by recognizing specific DNA motif, including those involved in invasion, antigenic variation, drug resistance, and sexual-stage development. Notably, normal genomic distribution pattern of AP2-P likewise depends on ARP1 or GCN5. Collectively, our study suggests a SAGA-like epigenetic module responsible for pathogenesis of Babesia gibsoni during asexual blood stage.

papers.title: Untitled
papers.abstract: Theileria annulata causes tropical theileriosis in cattle and is endemic in Kazakhstan. Although molecular diagnostic methods for this pathogen exist, data on its molecular surveillance and genetic diversity in Kazakhstan remain limited. This study aimed to develop and experimentally validate a species-specific real-time PCR (qPCR) assay for the detection of Theileria annulata and to conduct molecular surveillance and phylogenetic analysis of circulating isolates. A total of 709 cattle blood samples from 10 regions of Kazakhstan were analysed. Species-specific primers and a probe were designed targeting the 18S rRNA gene, and diagnostic performance was evaluated against sequencing as the reference method. Theileria annulata infection was confirmed in 110 of 709 samples (15.51%), with positive samples identified in the Turkistan, West Kazakhstan, Kyzylorda, and Zhambyl regions. The developed assay showed high diagnostic sensitivity (99.09%), specificity (99.67%), and diagnostic efficiency (99.58%), with no cross-reactivity with Theileria orientalis, Theileria parva, Babesia bovis, Babesia bigemina, or Anaplasma marginale. Phylogenetic analysis of partial 28S rRNA sequences confirmed the species identity of the detected isolates and demonstrated their close relationship with previously reported Kazakhstani and Chinese isolates. The developed qPCR assay is suitable for the molecular diagnosis and surveillance of bovine tropical theileriosis in Kazakhstan.

papers.title: Untitled
papers.abstract: Babesia is an intraerythrocytic parasite transmitted by ticks or through blood transfusion, and it can cause babesiosis with symptoms such as fever, anemia, and organ failure. The parasite is closely related to the mosquito-borne Plasmodium falciparum, which causes malaria. Several studies have shown that individuals with blood group O have a reduced risk of severe malaria compared to individuals with other ABO blood groups. Whether or not this is also the case for babesiosis has not yet been clearly investigated. In this study, serum samples from over 650 individuals were analyzed using an ELISA assay to detect antibodies against Babesia divergens. The ABO blood groups of the same samples were determined using a conventional method. There was no difference in B. divergens IgG antibody levels between the different ABO blood groups, nor was there any difference in the percentage of positive reactions in the ELISA against B. divergens between the different blood groups. This could indicate that the development and maintenance of B. divergens antibodies are not influenced by ABO blood groups.

papers.title: Impact of pharmacist-led prescribing for Lyme chemoprophylaxis on emergency department visits.
papers.abstract: All regions of Nova Scotia (NS) are considered at high risk for Lyme disease. Pharmacists in NS gained authority to prescribe chemoprophylaxis for the prevention of Lyme disease after a tick bite in August 2021. Our primary objective was to compare the frequency of emergency department (ED) visits for a tick bite before and after implementation of this expanded scope. A retrospective study using a pre-post design compared ED visits for tick bites 1.5 years before and 1.5 years after implementation of pharmacist prescribing. Patients who were assessed for a tick bite in 3 EDs were eligible for inclusion. Patients with active infection were excluded. Medical records were reviewed by research assistants. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize the data, and proportions of ED visits for tick bites were compared using the Chi-square test. A total of 1019 patient encounters for tick bites (617 pre-intervention vs 402 post-intervention) met inclusion criteria across 3 EDs. Of these, 67.7% (690/1019) resulted in a prescription for a single dose of doxycycline to prevent Lyme disease. After implementation, the frequency of patient encounters for tick bites declined by about half (617 encounters in 88,512 ED visits pre-intervention vs 402 encounters in 115,847 ED visits post-intervention [p < 0.0001]). After implementation of pharmacist prescribing for Lyme chemoprophylaxis, there was a decrease in patients visiting the ED for tick bites. Enabling pharmacist scope to include management of tick bites may alleviate some burden on local EDs in communities with high risk of Lyme disease.
papers.journal: Canadian pharmacists journal : CPJ = Revue des pharmaciens du Canada : RPC

papers.title: Visual outcomes and etiologic distribution of neuroretinitis: a 12-year retrospective study from a tertiary eye center.
papers.abstract: Neuroretinitis (NR) is a distinct optic neuropathy characterized by optic disc edema and macular exudates. Whether visual prognosis differs among etiologic subgroups remains unclear. This study aimed to retrospectively evaluate the demographic characteristics, etiologic distribution, and treatment outcomes of patients diagnosed with NR. We retrospectively reviewed NR cases diagnosed between January 2010 and August 2022 at a tertiary referral center. Demographic data, etiologic work-up results, treatment modalities, and visual outcomes were analyzed. Fifty-eight episodes in 34 patients (mean age: 38.3 ± 12.3 years; F/M ratio: 1.25:1) were evaluated. Twenty-five patients had unilateral and nine had bilateral involvement; eight experienced recurrences. Initial visual acuity ranged from 3.0 to 0.1 logMAR (mean ± SD: 0.81 ± 0.64), and final visual acuity ranged from 2.0 to 0 logMAR (mean ± SD: 0.27 ± 0.42).Etiologies included Bartonella (n = 9), Toxoplasma (n = 9), Borrelia (n = 3), Brucella (n = 2), and Behçet's disease (n = 1); ten cases were idiopathic. Mean initial/final visual acuities were 0.45/0.02 logMAR (antibiotics only), 0.58/0.06 logMAR (antibiotics + oral steroids), 0.62/0.08 logMAR (pulse steroids + antibiotics), and 0.79/0.44 logMAR (steroids only), respectively. Infectious agents accounted for a high proportion of NR cases in our cohort, underscoring the need for comprehensive etiologic investigations. Despite appropriate antibiotic therapy, recurrences may occur. Steroid administration without concurrent antimicrobial treatment may adversely affect visual prognosis.
